correctness.rationale: Every first-force size-three wedge is R or M and stalls, proving the lower bound. Every successful four-set is among eight fourth-vertex completions reducing to five symmetry classes. The explicit arrival-time table verifies the exact synchronous recurrence for all \(n\ge5\) and yields the polynomial; two distinct exhaustive programs cross-check all four-sets in bounded ranges, with the C++ implementation also checking each arrival-time vector through \(n=300\). Finite checks are corroboration, not the general proof.

originality.rationale: Statement-level comparison: AIM 2007 proves the minimum cardinality four but not which four-sets work or their synchronous times. Chilakamarri 2011 and Hogben 2014 introduce and develop the timing framework and include examples, not the complete five-orbit and three-level multiplicity polynomial. Boyer 2018 studies counting of zero-forcing sets but not these time-weighted counts. published-finding corpus and web searches with aliases yielded no indexed exact competitor. Historical priority remains conditional on accessible literature.
residual_risks: Unindexed or inaccessible older papers, appendices or computational tables might duplicate some/all of the exact labelled-set distribution.
Search absence is not a mathematical proof of uniqueness.

value.rationale: The natural cyclic-prism family is a standard cubic Cartesian product with established \(Z=4\). That scalar invariant cannot tell which optimal four-vertex initial conditions work or their speed. The complete five-orbit, \(13n\) count and three-level time polynomial resolve these complementary classification questions uniformly, with parity dependence in the fastest-set multiplicity and explicit finite classification certificates. This is a structural infinite-family statement, not an unmotivated finite slice.
